title: 08 — Azure Service Bus & Messaging
html:
08 — Azure Service Bus & Messaging

Four messaging services that look similar and are not interchangeable. Choosing wrong is expensive to undo, so §1 is the most important section.

1. Choosing: Service Bus vs Event Grid vs Event Hubs vs Storage Queues

flowchart TD
    A[I need to move data between components] --> B{Is it a discrete<br/>business message that MUST<br/>be processed reliably?}
    B -->|Yes| C{Do I need ordering, sessions,<br/>transactions, scheduled delivery,<br/>or dead-lettering?}
    C -->|Yes| SB[⭐ Service Bus]
    C -->|No, simple work queue| SQ[Storage Queue<br/>cheaper, simpler]
    B -->|No| D{Is it a high-volume<br/>telemetry/event STREAM?}
    D -->|Yes| EH[Event Hubs<br/>millions/sec, replayable]
    D -->|No| E{Is it a reactive notification<br/>fanned out to subscribers?}
    E -->|Yes| EG[Event Grid<br/>push, near-real-time]
Service Bus Event Grid Event Hubs Storage Queue
Model Enterprise broker (queue/topic) Event routing / pub-sub Streaming ingestion log Simple queue
Unit A message (a command with intent) An event (something happened) An event in a partitioned stream A message
Throughput Thousands/s Very high Millions/s High
Ordering ✅ Sessions (FIFO) ❌ ✅ Per partition ❌ (best effort)
Delivery Peek-lock, at-least-once Push, at-least-once, retried up to 24h Pull, consumer-managed offsets At-least-once
Replay ❌ (consumed = gone) ❌ ✅ Retention window ❌
DLQ ✅ Built in ✅ (to storage) ❌ ❌ (poison queue by convention)
Transactions ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌
Scheduled delivery ✅ ❌ ❌ ✅ (visibility timeout)
Max message size 256 KB (Std) / 100 MB (Premium) 🔄 1 MB 1 MB 64 KB
Cost £££ £ ££ ⭐ Cheapest
Use for Orders, payments, workflow commands "Blob created", "resource changed", reactive glue Telemetry, IoT, clickstream, logs Simple background jobs

💡 The combined pattern worth knowing: Event Grid for reactive routing (a blob was created) delivering into a Service Bus queue for reliable, ordered processing with dead-lettering. You get Event Grid's near-real-time push and Service Bus's processing guarantees.

⚠️ The classic mis-selection: using Event Hubs for business commands (no dead-lettering, no per-message retry — a poison event blocks the partition), or using Service Bus for telemetry (cost and throughput ceiling).

2. Service Bus concepts

Namespace  (the DNS-addressable boundary; a Premium namespace = dedicated capacity)
├── Queue                      point-to-point, competing consumers
└── Topic                      publish/subscribe
    ├── Subscription A  ── filter: sql/correlation ──► its own DLQ
    └── Subscription B  ── filter ──────────────────► its own DLQ
Concept Meaning
Queue One message → exactly one consumer. Multiple consumers compete (horizontal scale)
Topic + subscription One message → a copy per matching subscription. Each subscription behaves like its own queue
Peek-lock ⭐ The default receive mode: the message is locked, not deleted, until you Complete it
Lock duration Default 30 s, max 5 min. Renewable
Max delivery count After N failed deliveries → dead-letter queue (default 10)
DLQ A sub-queue (<queue>/$DeadLetterQueue) holding poison and expired messages
Session A FIFO group keyed by SessionId; one consumer holds the session lock at a time
TTL Message expiry → dead-lettered (if configured)
Duplicate detection The broker discards a repeated MessageId within a time window (Standard+)
Scheduled messages Deliver at a future time — retries with backoff, reminders
Auto-forward Chain a queue/subscription into another entity

Tiers: Basic (queues only, no topics — rarely useful) → Standard (topics, shared capacity, throttling possible) → Premium (dedicated capacity, predictable latency, 100 MB messages, zone redundancy, VNet/private endpoint, geo-DR). 💡 Premium for production if latency predictability or private networking matters; Standard is fine for moderate workloads.

3. ⭐ Peek-lock: the receive loop that matters

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Consumer
    participant Q as Queue
    C->>Q: Receive (peek-lock)
    Q-->>C: message + lock (30s default)
    Note over C: process...
    alt success
        C->>Q: Complete → message deleted
    else transient failure
        C->>Q: Abandon → lock released, deliveryCount++, redelivered immediately
    else permanent failure
        C->>Q: DeadLetter(reason) → moved to the DLQ
    else needs more time
        C->>Q: RenewLock
    else consumer crashes / lock expires
        Note over Q: lock expires → deliveryCount++ → redelivered<br/>⚠️ possibly while you're STILL processing
    end

⚠️ The lock-expiry duplicate is the #1 Service Bus production bug. Your handler takes 45 seconds, the lock was 30 seconds — the broker redelivers to another consumer while the first one is still working. Both complete. You've charged the customer twice.

Three defences, use all of them:

  1. Renew the lock for long work (MaxAutoLockRenewalDuration).
  2. Keep handlers short — hand long work to a durable job and complete the message.
  3. Be idempotent — the only real guarantee.
await using var processor = client.CreateProcessor("trades", new ServiceBusProcessorOptions
{
    MaxConcurrentCalls = 8,
    AutoCompleteMessages = false,                          // settle explicitly — always
    MaxAutoLockRenewalDuration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5),  // covers slow handlers
    PrefetchCount = 0,                                     // ⚠️ see §6
    ReceiveMode = ServiceBusReceiveMode.PeekLock
});

processor.ProcessMessageAsync += async args =>
{
    var message = args.Message;
    using var scope = logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
    {
        ["MessageId"] = message.MessageId,
        ["CorrelationId"] = message.CorrelationId ?? "none",
        ["DeliveryCount"] = message.DeliveryCount,
    });

    try
    {
        var trade = message.Body.ToObjectFromJson<TradeMessage>();
        await handler.HandleAsync(trade, args.CancellationToken);   // idempotent
        await args.CompleteMessageAsync(message, args.CancellationToken);
    }
    catch (JsonException ex)                        // permanent: malformed. Retrying can't help.
    {
        await args.DeadLetterMessageAsync(message, "DeserializationFailed", ex.Message);
    }
    catch (ValidationException ex)                  // permanent: business-invalid
    {
        await args.DeadLetterMessageAsync(message, "ValidationFailed", ex.Message);
    }
    catch (Exception ex)                            // transient: let the broker redeliver
    {
        logger.LogWarning(ex, "Transient failure on {MessageId}, delivery {Count}",
            message.MessageId, message.DeliveryCount);
        await args.AbandonMessageAsync(message);
    }
};

processor.ProcessErrorAsync += args =>
{
    logger.LogError(args.Exception, "Service Bus error in {Source} on {Entity}",
        args.ErrorSource, args.EntityPath);
    return Task.CompletedTask;
};

await processor.StartProcessingAsync(stoppingToken);

💡 Classify exceptions explicitly. Retrying a malformed message ten times wastes throughput and delays everything behind it; not retrying a transient database timeout loses valid work. The catch blocks above are the design.

4. Ordering with sessions

Without sessions, competing consumers process in parallel and ordering is lost. Sessions give FIFO within a session key, while still allowing parallelism across keys.

// Sender: the session id is the ordering key — usually your entity id
await sender.SendMessageAsync(new ServiceBusMessage(payload)
{
    SessionId = portfolioId.ToString(),        // all messages for one portfolio are ordered
    MessageId = outboxId.ToString(),           // for duplicate detection + consumer dedupe
    CorrelationId = correlationId,
    ContentType = "application/json",
    ApplicationProperties = { ["EventType"] = "TradeApproved", ["SchemaVersion"] = 1 }
});

// Receiver
await using var processor = client.CreateSessionProcessor("trades", new ServiceBusSessionProcessorOptions
{
    MaxConcurrentSessions = 8,          // 8 sessions in parallel...
    MaxConcurrentCallsPerSession = 1,   // ...but strictly one at a time within each
    SessionIdleTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)
});

⚠️ Session trade-offs: a session is locked to one consumer, so a single hot session (one very busy portfolio) becomes a throughput bottleneck. And if a message in a session fails and is abandoned repeatedly, the whole session stalls — everything behind it waits. Decide deliberately: strict ordering or throughput.

💡 The pragmatic alternative to sessions: make the consumer order-insensitive with a version number on the entity — apply an event only if event.Version > entity.Version. Out-of-order and duplicate events become no-ops, and you keep full parallelism.

5. Topics, subscriptions and filters

// Publisher doesn't know or care who is listening
await topicSender.SendMessageAsync(new ServiceBusMessage(json)
{
    Subject = "TradeApproved",
    ApplicationProperties = { ["Region"] = "UK", ["Notional"] = 5_000_000m }
});
Filter type Example Cost
Correlation filter Subject = "TradeApproved" and/or property equality ⭐ Cheapest — optimised index
SQL filter Region = 'UK' AND Notional > 1000000 More expensive to evaluate
True filter Everything (the default) — 
resource subscription 'Microsoft.ServiceBus/namespaces/topics/subscriptions@2022-10-01-preview' = {
  parent: topic
  name: 'risk-engine'
  properties: {
    maxDeliveryCount: 5
    deadLetteringOnMessageExpiration: true
    lockDuration: 'PT1M'
    defaultMessageTimeToLive: 'P7D'
  }
}
resource rule '...subscriptions/rules@2022-10-01-preview' = {
  parent: subscription
  name: 'large-uk-trades'
  properties: {
    filterType: 'CorrelationFilter'
    correlationFilter: { subject: 'TradeApproved', properties: { Region: 'UK' } }
  }
}

💡 Prefer correlation filters and put the routing keys in ApplicationProperties — the broker can filter without deserialising the body, which is both faster and cheaper. ⚠️ Remember to delete the default $Default true-filter rule when you add your own, or the subscription receives everything anyway.

6. Performance and throughput

Lever Effect Caveat
MaxConcurrentCalls Parallelism per consumer instance ⚠️ Multiply by instance count — match it to downstream capacity
PrefetchCount Fetch messages ahead of time — big latency win ⚠️ Prefetched messages hold their locks. If the consumer is slow, they expire and get redelivered. Set it to ~ (concurrency × messages processed per lock duration), or leave 0 until you've measured
Batching (SendMessagesAsync) Far fewer round trips Batch size limited by the max message size
Connection reuse ⭐ One ServiceBusClient per namespace, as a singleton Creating one per message is a classic and severe mistake
Partitioned entities More throughput Some feature restrictions
Premium tier Predictable latency, dedicated capacity Cost 
// ✔ Singleton client, sender per entity — both are thread-safe and poolable
builder.Services.AddAzureClients(clients =>
{
    clients.AddServiceBusClientWithNamespace("sb-shop-prod.servicebus.windows.net")
           .WithName("primary");
    clients.UseCredential(new DefaultAzureCredential());
});

// Batching
using var batch = await sender.CreateMessageBatchAsync(ct);
foreach (var evt in events)
    if (!batch.TryAddMessage(new ServiceBusMessage(Serialize(evt))))
    {
        await sender.SendMessagesAsync(batch, ct);   // batch full — send and start a new one
        // (create a new batch and re-add — omitted for brevity)
    }
await sender.SendMessagesAsync(batch, ct);

7. Reliability patterns

7.1 Transactional outbox (the one you'll use most)

The problem: you must update the database and publish a message. Two systems, no distributed transaction. Crash in between and you either lose the event or announce something that didn't happen.

BEGIN TRAN
  UPDATE trades SET status = 'Approved' WHERE id = @id;
  INSERT INTO outbox (id, event_type, payload, occurred_at) VALUES (...);
COMMIT
-- A relay reads unpublished rows and sends them, using the outbox id as the MessageId

This gives at-least-once publishing — which is precisely why consumers must be idempotent. The alternative implementation is CDC (Debezium / SQL Server CDC tailing the log), which needs no polling and catches writes from every source.

7.2 Idempotent consumers

Two mechanisms, use whichever fits:

  • Broker-side duplicate detection: enable it on the entity with a detection window, and set a deterministic MessageId. Cheap, but the window is finite.
  • Consumer-side dedupe table: insert the message id in the same transaction as the effect, with a unique constraint. Bulletproof.

7.3 Dead-letter handling

Every queue and subscription needs: a sensible maxDeliveryCount (5–10), deadLetteringOnMessageExpiration: true, an alert on DLQ depth > 0, and a replay tool so reprocessing after a fix is one command, not archaeology.

// Reading the DLQ
var dlqReceiver = client.CreateReceiver("trades", new ServiceBusReceiverOptions
{
    SubQueue = SubQueue.DeadLetter
});
var messages = await dlqReceiver.ReceiveMessagesAsync(100, cancellationToken: ct);
foreach (var m in messages)
{
    logger.LogWarning("DLQ {Id}: {Reason} — {Description}",
        m.MessageId, m.DeadLetterReason, m.DeadLetterErrorDescription);
    // after fixing: re-send to the main queue, then complete on the DLQ receiver
}

⚠️ A silently filling DLQ is data loss with extra steps. Alerting on it is not optional.

7.4 Backpressure

If consumers can't keep up, the queue grows. Your options, and you must pick one deliberately: scale consumers (KEDA on queue depth is the cleanest — see file 06 §8), shed low-priority messages, rate-limit producers, or accept the lag and alert on it. Unbounded growth is not a strategy.

8. Message design

public sealed record TradeApproved(
    Guid            MessageId,        // idempotency key
    Guid            CorrelationId,    // ties back to the originating user request
    Guid?           CausationId,      // the message that caused this one
    DateTimeOffset  OccurredAt,       // EVENT time, not publish time
    int             SchemaVersion,    // version from message #1
    Guid            TradeId,
    string          PortfolioCode,
    decimal         Notional,
    string          Currency);

Rules:

  1. Past-tense names for events (TradeApproved); imperative for commands (ApproveTrade).
  2. Version from the first message. Adding a version field later is much harder.
  3. Additive changes only within a version. Removing or renaming a field, or changing its type or meaning, is breaking.
  4. Keep payloads small — use the claim-check pattern (store the blob, send the reference) for anything large.
  5. ⚠️ No secrets or full PII in a message — it's persisted, replicated, logged, and often replayable.
  6. Put routing keys in ApplicationProperties so subscriptions can filter without deserialising.

Schema evolution: a schema registry (Azure Schema Registry in Event Hubs) with backward-compatibility enforcement turns "we broke the consumers" from a production incident into a build failure. Worth it once more than one team consumes your events.

9. Event Grid

Push-based routing of discrete events, near-real-time, with built-in retry (exponential backoff over up to 24h) and optional dead-lettering to storage.

System topics publish Azure resource events for free: blob created/deleted, resource group changes, Key Vault secret near expiry, Media Services job complete, and many more.

resource blobSubscription 'Microsoft.EventGrid/systemTopics/eventSubscriptions@2023-12-15-preview' = {
  parent: storageSystemTopic
  name: 'trade-files-to-servicebus'
  properties: {
    destination: {                                  // ⭐ deliver INTO Service Bus for reliable processing
      endpointType: 'ServiceBusQueue'
      properties: { resourceId: tradeQueue.id }
    }
    filter: {
      includedEventTypes: ['Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated']
      subjectBeginsWith: '/blobServices/default/containers/incoming/'
      subjectEndsWith: '.csv'
    }
    retryPolicy: { maxDeliveryAttempts: 10, eventTimeToLiveInMinutes: 1440 }
    deadLetterDestination: {
      endpointType: 'StorageBlob'
      properties: { resourceId: storage.id, blobContainerName: 'eventgrid-dlq' }
    }
  }
}

⚠️ Webhook endpoints must complete the validation handshake (echo back the validationCode on the subscription-validation event) or the subscription never activates — a very common first-time failure.

⚠️ Event Grid delivery is at-least-once and unordered. Design handlers to be idempotent and order-insensitive.

💡 Use the Event Grid–based blob trigger for Functions rather than the polling blob trigger: the polling trigger can be minutes late on Consumption plans, which surprises people badly.

10. Event Hubs (briefly)

A partitioned, append-only log for streaming — telemetry, IoT, clickstream, logs. Kafka-protocol compatible.

Concept Meaning
Partition The unit of parallelism and ordering. ⚠️ Fixed at creation on lower tiers — choose carefully
Consumer group An independent view of the stream with its own offsets
Checkpoint The consumer's committed position, stored in a blob container
Capture Automatic archival to Blob/Data Lake in Avro — free-ish and very useful
Retention 1–7 days (Standard), longer on Premium/Dedicated 🔄 — this is what makes replay possible 
var processor = new EventProcessorClient(
    checkpointStore: blobContainerClient,
    consumerGroup: "risk-engine",
    fullyQualifiedNamespace: "eh-shop.servicebus.windows.net",
    eventHubName: "trades",
    credential: new DefaultAzureCredential());

processor.ProcessEventAsync += async args =>
{
    Process(args.Data);
    // ⚠️ Checkpoint periodically, NOT per event — checkpointing is a storage write
    if (++count % 100 == 0)
        await args.UpdateCheckpointAsync(args.CancellationToken);
};

⚠️ Consumer count must not exceed partition count — extra consumers sit idle. Partitions are the scale unit.

11. Storage Queues

The simplest option: a queue in a storage account. No topics, no sessions, no transactions, no DLQ — but very cheap and perfectly adequate for straightforward background work.

Use Storage Queue when Use Service Bus when
Simple work distribution Ordering, transactions, sessions, scheduling
Cost matters and volume is high Dead-lettering and per-message retry semantics matter
Messages are small and independent Pub/sub with filtered subscriptions
>80 GB of queued messages needed Duplicate detection needed

Poison-message handling is manual: the SDK/Functions binding tracks dequeueCount and moves the message to <queue>-poison after maxDequeueCount. Configure it and monitor that queue.

12. Monitoring

Metric Why it matters
Active message count The primary health signal
Age of the oldest message ⭐ Better than depth — catches a stalled consumer at low volume
Dead-letter message count Alert on > 0
Incoming vs outgoing messages Producer/consumer balance
Throttled requests You're exceeding the tier's capacity (Standard)
Server/user errors Auth failures, lock expiries
Scheduled message count Growth here can indicate a broken retry loop 
AzureMetrics
| where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.SERVICEBUS"
| where MetricName in ("ActiveMessages", "DeadletteredMessages")
| summarize avg(Average) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), MetricName, Resource
| render timechart

Trace propagation: HTTP trace context does not flow across a queue automatically. Inject traceparent into ApplicationProperties on send and restore it on receive, or your distributed trace stops exactly where you most need it. (The newer Azure SDKs do much of this for you — verify in your traces that the spans actually link.)

13. Checklist

  • Right service chosen: Service Bus for business messages, Event Grid for reactive routing, Event Hubs for streams, Storage Queue for cheap simple work
  • Managed identity + fullyQualifiedNamespace — no SAS connection strings
  • Singleton ServiceBusClient; senders and processors reused
  • AutoCompleteMessages = false — settle explicitly
  • Exceptions classified: permanent → dead-letter, transient → abandon
  • Lock duration and MaxAutoLockRenewalDuration exceed the realistic handler time
  • Consumers are idempotent — the mechanism is written down
  • Ordering requirement decided: sessions, or version-based order-insensitivity
  • maxDeliveryCount, TTL, and deadLetteringOnMessageExpiration set on every entity
  • Alert on DLQ depth > 0 and on oldest-message age
  • Replay tooling for the DLQ exists and has been used at least once
  • Concurrency and prefetch tuned against downstream capacity
  • Outbox (or CDC) wherever a DB write and a publish must agree
  • Messages carry id, correlation id, occurred-at, and schema version; no PII or secrets
  • Correlation/trace context propagated across the queue
  • Premium tier + zone redundancy for production if latency or private networking matters

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • Service Bus vs Event Hubs vs Event Grid? Reliable discrete business messages with ordering, transactions and DLQ / high-volume replayable streams / reactive push notifications with fan-out. Say what each can't do.
  • What is peek-lock and what goes wrong with it? The message is locked rather than deleted until you settle it. If processing outlasts the lock, it's redelivered while you're still working — hence lock renewal, short handlers, and idempotency.
  • How do you guarantee ordering while scaling consumers? Sessions keyed by entity id — ordered within a session, parallel across sessions. Then name the cost: a hot session bottlenecks, and a failing message stalls the whole session.
  • Can you achieve exactly-once? Not as delivery. At-least-once plus idempotent consumers gives an exactly-once effect; the idempotency key is the design decision.
  • How do you reliably publish an event when you also write to the database? Transactional outbox or CDC. Never dual-write.
  • A message keeps failing. What happens? Bounded redelivery via maxDeliveryCount, then the DLQ, then an alert and human triage — never an infinite loop.

Sources: Architecture best practices for Azure Service Bus — Azure Well-Architected Framework · Event Grid vs Service Bus vs Event Hubs comparison · Azure Service Bus with .NET
